newsitem.title: USA: Seagate to pay in Amstrad suit, take charge.
newsitem.headline: Seagate to pay in Amstrad suit, take charge.

text.p: Seagate Technology Inc., one of the world's largest makers of computer disk drives, said Friday an English court awarded $93 million to Amstrad Plc in a lawsuit over allegedly faulty disk drives.
Interest and other costs could push the award $60 million higher, Seagate said in a statement.
Amstrad said in its statement issued from London it would apply for the interest.

Seagate plans to take a charge of "a like amount" in the current quarter ending in June, which is the company's fourth quarter of fiscal 1997. A spokeswoman said by "like amount" the company meant the award of $93 million plus the estimated $60 million in interest and other costs.
Seagate officials were unavailable to comment.
Seagate also plans to appeal the decision, which was handed down Friday by the High Court of Justice in England.
The award did little to dampen enthusiasm over Seagate's stock in trading on Wall Street. Shares of the high-technology company rose 87.5 cents to $51.75.

Financial analysts said the lawsuit was more of nuisance than a product performance issue for the Silicon Valley-based company because it centres on products made in the late 1980s whose technology is no longer used.
"It's really an immaterial issue," said Paul Fox, analyst at Montgomery Securities.

Seagate's annual revenues generate are well over $9 billion, and in its most recent quarter ended March 31, the company posted net income of more than $250 million. Seagate employs more than 100,000 people in 22 countries.
The case originates from allegedly defective drives Seagate sold to Amstrad in the 1988-1989 time frame. Amstrad brought the action in 1992, and the trial took place last year.
Amstrad is also taking action against Western Digital Corp., again for faulty computer disk drives, with a trial set for later this year in California.
In a statement, Western Digital noted the underlying facts of the two cases are different because Seagate in its case acknowledged a design flaw but disputed the significance.
Western Digital, however, said Amstrad has yet to identify the exact defect it claims were in the drives.

A Western Digital spokesman said the company's drives in question numbered about 70,000 and were sold to Amstrad in 1988 and 1989. He noted the drives are no longer sold because their technology is outdated. Western Digital stock rose $1.125 to $70.50 on the NYSE.
